desc:
A road network has cities 0 to n - 1 and bidirectional roads edges[i] = [u, v, w] of length w (several roads may join the same two cities). Each query [p, q, limit] asks: is there a route from p to q in which every road has length strictly less than limit?

Return an array with one entry per query: 1 if such a route exists, otherwise 0. A query with p = q is always answered 1.

n = 5
edges = [[0,1,2],[1,2,4],[2,3,6],[0,3,10],[3,4,1]]
queries = [[0,2,5],[0,3,6],[0,3,7],[4,4,1],[3,4,1],[3,4,2]]

result = [1,0,1,1,0,1]
constraints: edges[i] = [u, v, w] with 0 ≤ u, v < n, u ≠ v and 1 ≤ w ≤ 10<sup>6</sup>
queries[j] = [p, q, limit] with 0 ≤ p, q < n and 1 ≤ limit ≤ 10<sup>6</sup> + 1
hints: Running a BFS that ignores long roads for each query is O(queries · (n + edges)). Look for a way to share work between queries.
Different queries differ only in how many roads are allowed. If you handle queries in order of increasing limit, the allowed road set only grows.

Sort the roads by length and the queries by limit. For each query in that order, union all roads with length < limit not yet added, then check find(p) == find(q). Store the answer at the original query index.
editorial: The set of usable roads for a query is 'all roads shorter than limit'. If the queries are sorted by limit, these sets are nested: each query uses all the roads of the previous one plus a few more. That is exactly the situation where union-find shines, because it only supports merging.

Sort the roads by weight, sort the query indices by limit, and keep a pointer into the road list. For each query (in increasing limit) advance the pointer while the next road has w < limit, uniting its endpoints. The query is then answered by comparing the roots of p and q; write the answer into the slot of the original query. Total time is O(E log E + Q log Q + (E + Q) · α(n)). Answering queries offline in a clever order is the whole trick.
time: O(E log E + Q log Q)
